With speed comes risk.

Also, a racing circuit's speed will generally increase as more rubber gets laid down on it. All other things being equal, that makes the end of the session the best condition to achieve the fastest possible lap.

In qualifying, it's much better to put in a 'banker' lap at, say, 80 or 90% effort in order to have a time recorded than to only wait until the end of the session to do the 100% lap.

Additionally, changing conditions can negatively affect the circuit's speed (track temperature, wind gusts, rain), and it's always possible to have an incident causing caution flags or stoppages.

Putting in a 'banker' lap allows the team to mitigate those risks without too much at stake (generally just a set of tires).

On pace, they were lapping similarly to mid-tier endurance racing cars. They were much faster on the straights, but slower in the corners.

The biggest root issue that affected their pace was the fact that they didn't have operational energy recovery systems. They intended to use a flywheel to recover energy in braking zones, but couldn't get it working. This is especially important, since it's front weight-biased (60%+). At one point, I thought I heard that there was some miscommunication or exaggerated specification by the flywheel provider.

Anyway, since they couldn't use the flywheel, that means that the brakes they had intended to use had to do the full job of stopping the car. They fitted some larger brakes, but those wouldn't fit under the wheels they were going to run. They fitted larger wheels, but that then meant that they couldn't use the bespoke tyres made for them to handle the huge amount of acceleration, braking, and turning that their fronts have to do. They ended up using the standard tyres for their class.

They also had to swap their brakes much more frequently. I think it was in a video that they intended to do a brake replacement once, and hopefully not at all. They ended up doing their first brake replacement in hour 6.

The other reasons they were so low were due to the times spent in the pits. One started from the pits due to a clutch issue. Another car had an extended repair session after hitting what appears to be an obstacle while on the straight that damaged front suspension and the transmission. I think two times they replaced a sensor provided by the governing body (I'd guess fuel flow, or something). They made it known that they were treating this as a full-scale testing session, so they seemed to pit more frequently than they would in a true race scenario, just to do extra checks.

Betteridge's law of headlines states that any headline that ends in a question mark can be answered with the word "no." This principle suggests that if a headline poses a question, it is likely that the answer is negative or that the content does not support a positive response. This law is often referenced in discussions about journalism and media, highlighting the tendency for sensationalism in headlines.

Now they're talking about progress non-stop, and how can anyone blame them for that? There's no point rubbing anyone's face in their result, since they didn't fail. You'll hear it in any racing series - Everyone's "just focusing on getting the best possible result at the next race" or "learning from the experience and finding opportunities for improvement." They were given a (to be nice) less-than-stellar power unit by their supplier, and they called them out repeatedly and publicly, as if to shame them or force them to do better. They complained much more loudly than another team did about their own supplier. Most people didn't like this approach. It creates friction within the team, and between the team and its suppliers.

Another team mentioned that there was some sort of miscommunication about the flywheel's capability, or perhaps over-promising specs. If that's the case, why should the other team call them out as a reason for being off the pace? They had/have enough of their own issues to work out, so that's what they focused on, and rightfully so.

To sum up, I don't know the list of, nor the extent of the issues faced at the recent event, but I don't believe that it's fair to write off a racing effort after a single race, nor do I feel like I deserve an apology from the team.

One advancement of modern engines is reducing the time to warm up the engine.

Cold engines have cold oil, which doesn't lubricate as well.

The faster the vehicle warms up, the quicker the oil reaches a temperature where it can fully protect all of the moving parts inside the engine, and also, the faster the emissions control system warms up and starts being effective at reducing tailpipe emissions.

The cold oil problem is why it's a bad idea to ask a lot of your engine when it's cold (either by applying a lot of load or high revs or both).

I don't know what specific advances lead to raising the engine (and thus oil) temperature quickly, but one progression that has happened from the emissions control perspective is moving the catalyst ever closer to the engine cylinders themselves.
